name: AD9851BRSZRL
title: AD9851 CMOS 180 MHz DDS/DAC synthesizer
summary: A direct digital synthesizer: a 32-bit tuning word and 5-bit phase word set a sine wave generated from a clock of up to 180 MHz, made analog by an on-chip 10-bit DAC. A built-in comparator with hysteresis can square the filtered sine into a low-jitter CMOS clock, and a 6× reference multiplier lets a 30 MHz reference run the core at 180 MHz. The 40-bit control word loads over an 8-bit parallel bus or serially on one pin. It runs from 2.7 V to 5.25 V in a 28-lead SSOP, pin compatible with the AD9850.
key_figures: 180 MHz max at 5 V; 125 MHz at 3.3 V; 100 MHz at 2.7 V
43 dBc typ at 70.1 MHz out; 64 dBc typ at 1.1 MHz
555 mW typ at 180 MHz, 5 V; power-down 4 mW typ at 2.7 V
–40°C to +85°C above 3.0 V; 0°C to 85°C below 3.0 V

pins.name: D3
pins.function: Data bus bit 3 of the 8-bit parallel port.

pins.name: D2
pins.function: Data bus bit 2. Turns into an output if the factory test mode is entered by mistake; RESET leaves that mode.

pins.name: D1
pins.function: Data bus bit 1.

pins.name: D0
pins.function: Data bus bit 0, the LSB.

pins.name: PGND
pins.function: Ground for the 6× REFCLK multiplier.

pins.name: PVCC
pins.function: Supply for the 6× REFCLK multiplier.

pins.name: W_CLK
pins.function: Word load clock. Each rising edge writes a parallel byte or a serial bit into the 40-bit input register, independent of the reference clock.

pins.name: FQ_UD
pins.function: Frequency update. A rising edge hands the 40-bit input register to the DDS core and returns the word pointer to W0. Issue it only when the register holds known, valid data.

pins.name: REFCLOCK
pins.function: Reference clock, a CMOS/TTL pulse train. Used directly as the system clock, or multiplied by 6 when the multiplier is on, in which case the multiplier output is the system clock. Operations start on the system clock rising edge.

pins.name: AGND
pins.function: Ground return for the analog circuits, DAC and comparator.

pins.name: AVDD
pins.function: Analog supply for the bandgap reference.

pins.name: RSET
pins.function: Resistor to ground sets the DAC full-scale current at IOUT and IOUTB; 3.92 kΩ nominally gives 10 mA. RSET = 39.93/IOUT.

pins.name: VOUTN
pins.function: Comparator complementary CMOS-level output.

pins.name: VOUTP
pins.function: Comparator true CMOS-level output.

pins.name: VINN
pins.function: Comparator inverting input.

pins.name: VINP
pins.function: Comparator noninverting input.

pins.name: DACBP
pins.function: Bypass point of the DAC voltage reference. Normally left unconnected, which gives the best SFDR.

pins.name: AVDD
pins.function: Analog supply for the DAC and comparator.

pins.name: AGND
pins.function: Ground return for the analog circuits, DAC and comparator.

pins.name: IOUTB
pins.function: Complementary DAC current output: full scale minus IOUT. Load it the same as IOUT for the best SFDR.

pins.name: IOUT
pins.function: True DAC output, a sourcing current: full scale minus IOUTB. Needs conversion to voltage, usually a resistor or transformer returned to ground.

pins.name: RESET
pins.function: Master reset, active high. Zeroes the phase accumulator and phase offset (0 Hz, 0°), selects parallel loading and turns the 6× multiplier off; the 40-bit input register keeps its contents. Assert it first after power-up, before any programming.

pins.name: DVDD
pins.function: Digital supply.

pins.name: DGND

pins.function: Data bus bit 7, the MSB; also the input for the 40-bit serial word.

circuits.title: Basic clock generator configuration
circuits.description: The DAC sine wave is turned into a square wave by the on-chip comparator. IOUT drives a 70 MHz seventh-order elliptic low-pass filter of 200 Ω impedance, terminated with 200 Ω at both ends, so 10 mA full scale gives a 0 to 1 V p-p sine at the filter output, which goes to VINP. IOUTB carries an equal 100 Ω load. Two 100 kΩ resistors average the IOUT and IOUTB voltages and the 470 pF capacitor smooths the result into a dc level at the middle of the sine wave, about 0.5 V, which sets the threshold on VINN. The comparator then switches near 50% duty cycle. RSET of 3.9 kΩ sets the full-scale current; a microprocessor loads the part over the data bus, and the reference clock is 180 MHz direct or 30 MHz with the 6× multiplier.

parts.value: 70 MHz 7th-order elliptical low-pass filter, 200 Ω impedance

notes: The bus carries either 8-bit parallel data or 40 serial bits on D7, with RESET, W_CLK and FQ_UD.

circuits.title: Differential DAC output through a transformer
circuits.description: IOUT and IOUTB drive the ends of a 1:1 transformer primary whose centre tap is grounded; the secondary, returned to ground, feeds the output filter, which is terminated by 50 Ω at the output connector. Driving the transformer differentially cancels common-mode signals and lets a reactive filter run without a termination resistor at its input. Because the filter is only terminated at one end, its output has 6 dB more power than the single-ended connection.

parts.note: pins P1, P2 primary ends, PCT primary centre tap, S1, S2 secondary

circuits.title: RSET driven by an external DAC for amplitude control
circuits.description: A 10-bit current-output DAC (AD9731, up to 20 mA) loaded by 330 Ω to +5 V and 200 Ω to ground sets a voltage that drives RSET through 4 kΩ, so the DAC code sets the AD9851 full-scale output current, either modulating the amplitude or holding it at a digitally chosen level. A data generator feeds the 10-bit DAC; one 125 MHz clock source clocks both the DAC and REFCLOCK, and a computer loads the AD9851. The output is taken differentially through a 1:1 transformer with a 50 Ω load. With the 6× multiplier on, the 125 MHz clock can be six times lower.

parts.note: pins P1, P2 primary ends, PCT primary centre tap, S1, S2 secondary

notes: The AD9851 runs from +5 V; its control lines come from the computer.

circuits.title: Hardwired xxxxx011 serial-enable word
circuits.description: D0 and D1 are tied together and pulled to the supply through 10 kΩ, and D2 is grounded, so the bus always presents xxxxx011. One W_CLK edge followed by FQ_UD then switches the part from parallel to serial loading, after which serial data enters on D7.
notes: D3 to D7 have no connection in this circuit.

circuits.title: AD9851/FSPCB frequency synthesizer evaluation board
circuits.description: Evaluation board for the AD9851 as a frequency synthesizer. A PC printer port on J1 drives two 74HCT574 latches: U2 holds the data byte for D0 to D7 and U3 holds RESET, W_CLK and FQ_UD, both clocked by STROBE, with 2.2 kΩ pull-ups to 5 V on the port lines. The unfiltered DAC output IOUT is loaded with 50 Ω and brought to the J6 BNC for a 50 Ω analyzer; IOUTB is loaded with 25 Ω. The comparator is reached through test points, its inputs held apart by 1 kΩ to +V (VINN) and 1 kΩ to ground (VINP) so it does not chatter when unused. The clock enters at J5 into 50 Ω, or comes from an optional oscillator Y1 once R2 is removed. The AD9851 runs from +V (J2), the latches and oscillator from 5 V (J3); each rail has a 10 µF tantalum and 0.1 µF ceramics.

circuits.title: AD9851/CGPCB clock generator evaluation board
circuits.description: Evaluation board for the AD9851 as a CMOS clock generator. The digital side matches the FSPCB board: J1 from a PC printer port into two 74HCT574 latches clocked by STROBE, 2.2 kΩ pull-ups, J5 clock input with 50 Ω (R2) or an optional oscillator Y1, +V for the AD9851 and 5 V for the rest. IOUT goes to the J7 BNC and, through jumper E5-E6, into a 70 MHz seventh-order elliptic low-pass filter of 200 Ω impedance (L1 to L3 with C11 to C17), terminated with 200 Ω at both ends. Jumper E3-E4 takes the filter output to VINP (also on J6). R4 and R5, 100 kΩ each, average IOUT and IOUTB (loaded with 100 Ω); jumper E1-E2 brings that midpoint, filtered by 470 pF, to VINN as the switching threshold. The comparator outputs are on J8 and J9. Removing the jumpers lets a user fit their own filter between J7 and J6 and supply a threshold at E1; R12 then terminates IOUT.

operation.text: A numerically controlled oscillator: a 32-bit phase accumulator adds the tuning word on every system clock and wraps at full scale, so a bigger word wraps sooner and gives a higher frequency. A proprietary angle-rotation algorithm turns 14 truncated phase bits into a 10-bit amplitude with a small ROM table, and a 10-bit DAC makes the analog sine wave. Frequency changes are phase-continuous. An on-chip comparator can square the filtered sine into a low-jitter CMOS/TTL clock.
Five phase bits shift the output in 11.25° steps.

An internal multiplier lets a low-frequency reference (5 MHz minimum, 30 MHz at 5 V for a 180 MHz system clock) replace a fast oscillator. It is switched on by bit data[0] of W0 in parallel loading or W32 in serial loading, and RESET turns it off. With it on, overall phase noise generally rises, from its 6× (15.5 dB) phase gain and its own internal noise.

Below 1 MHz without the multiplier, or 5 MHz with it, internal circuitry senses the slow clock and puts the part into power-down, comparator included; the comparator is then unusable for other jobs. When the clock comes back above the threshold the part resumes after typically 5 µs. The shutdown keeps the dynamic registers from leaking excessive current.

The output is a sampled signal: besides the fundamental it carries images at each multiple of the system clock plus and minus the output frequency, shaped by a sin(x)/x roll-off. Usable bandwidth is dc to half the system clock; at fOUT equal to half the clock the first image is as large as the fundamental. A low-pass filter normally sits between DAC and comparator. Images move 1:1 with the fundamental; the one below a clock multiple moves the opposite way, the one above moves the same way. With a band-pass filter and amplification an image can be the output (for example 240 MHz from a 30 MHz clock with the multiplier), though spurious content near images is higher.
Keep the fundamental at or below 40% of the reference clock frequency so that aliases stay far enough from the wanted band to be filtered cheaply.

Dividing down the clock lowers its phase noise at the output by 20 log(fOUT/fCLK), so a high system clock helps. With a low phase noise reference the output is better than –100 dBc/Hz up to 50 MHz output for offsets of 1 kHz to 100 kHz.

A 40-bit register holds the 32-bit tuning word, 5 phase bits, the multiplier enable, the power-down bit and a test bit; a 1 engages a function. It loads in parallel (five bytes) or serially (40 bits on D7). Bit data[1] of W0, or W33 in serial loading, selects a factory test mode and must stay 0; if entered (pin 2 becomes an output), RESET exits it. The power-up contents of the register are random and RESET does not clear them, so FQ_UD must not be pulsed until the register has been written with known data, or the part may enter test or power-down mode.

The default after RESET. Each W_CLK rising edge writes the next byte, W0 first, then W1 to W4; edges after W4 are ignored until RESET or FQ_UD returns the pointer to W0. FQ_UD's rising edge moves the register into the core. Words are loaded in sequence only: W0 can be updated alone followed by FQ_UD, but changing W1 needs W0 then W1.

Entered from parallel mode by writing W0 = xxxxx011 (over the bus or hardwired) with one W_CLK edge, then FQ_UD. Then 40 W_CLK edges shift bits W0 to W39 in from D7; further edges shift data out and corrupt it. Right after entering serial mode, write a valid 40-bit word (W33 = 0, even all zeros) and pulse FQ_UD, so that the leftover parallel byte does not turn on the multiplier or test mode. Only RESET returns to parallel mode.

RESET zeroes the phase accumulator (0 Hz, dc out) and the phase offset, so IOUT sits at full scale and IOUTB at zero. It returns the address pointer to W0, clears the power-down bit, turns the multiplier off and selects parallel loading. The 40-bit input register is not cleared: a FQ_UD after RESET reloads the earlier word, which takes effect 18 clock cycles later.
Set bit data[2] of W0 (parallel) or W34 (serial) to 1 and pulse FQ_UD; internal clocks stop. Clearing it restarts the part in about 5 µs. The input register can be written while powered down.

Several AD9851s clocked from the same reference are first RESET together, then each 40-bit register is written with its own W_CLK while sharing the data bus; a common FQ_UD starts all of them at once with their programmed frequency and phase, for example two parts 90° apart as a quadrature oscillator.
Driving RSET from an external DAC gives amplitude modulation or digital amplitude setting of the DAC output current.

Applications: chip-rate clock generator locked to a spread-spectrum transmitter for ADC encoding; frequency- and phase-agile local oscillator for mixing; agile reference for a PLL; programmable divide-by-N in a PLL; all-digital FM generation with a DSP; image-based high-frequency output.

Use a multilayer board with dedicated power and ground planes kept as free of cuts as possible, and a ground fill on the top layer so surface-mount parts reach ground without vias. Separate analog and digital grounds join at the AD9851. Keep digital lines from running under the part, use wide supply traces, route fast clocks as controlled-impedance microstrip, keep analog and digital paths from crossing, and run traces on opposite sides at right angles. AVDD and DVDD pins are separate; decouple analog pins to AGND and digital pins to DGND with ceramic chip capacitors close to the part. Where one supply feeds both, use the system's analog supply.

Band-pass filtering the DAC output, where only a narrow band is needed, removes spurs either side of the wanted signal and lowers jitter. A lower supply reduces comparator switching noise. For the lowest jitter an external fast comparator avoids the noisy digital surroundings of the on-chip one.

The AD9851/FSPCB is for synthesizer use, with an unfiltered DAC output for a 50 Ω analyzer and no oscillator fitted. The AD9851/CGPCB is for clock generation, with the 70 MHz 200 Ω elliptic filter between DAC and comparator; at 10 mA it develops 1 V p-p across the 200 Ω terminations, enough for the comparator, and the filter assumes a 180 MHz clock. The DUT supply takes 2.7 V to 5.25 V and may be tied to the 5 V supply. A sine generator can clock the board above 50 MHz if offset to half the supply, at least 2 V p-p, with the multiplier off. After RESET, IOUT shows a dc level equal to full scale (1 V on the CGPCB, 0.5 V on the FSPCB) and IOUTB 0 V.
Pin-for-pin compatible with the AD9850 125 MHz DDS. Programming differs only in data[0] of W0 (parallel) or W32 (serial), which is now the 6× multiplier enable.
